transcript:
Meeting header: 2028-03-14 15:00 UTC — Duration 47 mins
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Luis (CSM) — Helixa: Rajiv (CTO), Lina (ML Lead), Omar (SRE), Sophie (PM)

[00:00] Jordan: alright, thanks everyone for joining, we'll keep to 45 minutes, quick agenda — run through the benchmark delta vs your incumbent, highlight where p95 creeps up, talk mitigation (routing, cache, quantize) and agree next steps.
[00:23] Rajiv: thanks, Jordan. we've got limited time, so straight to the numbers please, Lina has the context for inference types.
[00:35] Lina: yeah we're mostly concerned with the long-context clinical summarization flow, 8k tokens, synchronous API calls from our annotators. baseline vendor currently at ~420ms median, 1.2s p95 under our 1k conc load.
[00:50] Maya: ok, thanks. for the Redwood runs we replayed your traffic and ran identical prompts — median improved to ~320ms but p95 is trending 950ms to 1.05s on the 8k flows. short prompts (<=1k tokens) p95 is clean under 400ms.
[01:15] Omar: quick question, is that cold KV cache or warm? our production is a mix and the first few minutes spike.
[01:25] Maya: good point — the reported p95 includes a warmup period; if you look at steady-state after 20 minutes the p95 narrows to ~820ms. We called out KV cash — sorry, KV cache — warming behaviour in the notes, there's an initial prefix cache miss pattern.
[01:42] Lina: 820ms is better than 1.2s baseline but we care about tails, especially for sync UX. what are the levers? quantize? smaller sequence splits?
[01:55] Maya: levers are: 1) routing to faster model variants for short tails, 2) dedicated slots pinned to your traffic with larger KV cache residency, 3) quantization trade-offs (int8) which shave compute but can add slight generation jitter, and 4) batching policy tweaks.
[02:14] Jordan: and on cost tradeoffs — dedicated slots reduce p95 variability but are a committed cost; we sketched a burst + dedicated hybrid in the deck.
[02:27] Sophie: can you remind us how routing works if a slot is saturated? do we fallback to the baseline vendor?
[02:35] Maya: we fallback to compatible model variants or a lower-cost pool in-region. we don't automatically send traffic to third-party vendors unless configured, but you can set a multi-tier routing policy to route to your incumbent during incidents.
[02:52] Rajiv: hmm, interesting. security: our infosec asked about KMS for key handling and if Redwood keeps any copies of inputs.
[03:02] Jordan: Redwood does not retain customer-request bodies outside of short-lived logs unless configured. We'll supply SOC2 and the KMS integration guide; we support customer-managed KMS for Private.
[03:15] Omar: for peering we need a network diagram — particularly interested in egress flows and if there are any managed NAT hops.
[03:25] Jordan: noted, will attach diagram.
[03:30] 
[03:30] Maya: diving deeper into the p95 regression — the primary pattern we saw was a mix of token-level compute spikes for long contexts and periodic cache evictions when concurrency crosses a threshold. We include a heatmap in the spreadsheet: you can see tokens/sec vs slot memory pressure.
[03:55] Lina: can you explain 'cache eviction' in plain terms for our product folks?
[04:02] Maya: sure — think of KV cache as per-session memory for the past tokens; when too many sessions compete for limited residency, older sessions get evicted and must be recomputed — that recompute shows up as a tail spike.
[04:18] Rajiv: what's the suggested threshold to avoid eviction? we run bursts of 1k concurrent around noon daily.
[04:26] Maya: our rule of thumb from these runs is keep residency >1.5x your 95th concurrent sessions. for your workload that suggests moving to a dedicated pool with a slightly larger slot size and adjusted eviction policy.
[04:41] Omar: what's the expected delta in unit cost if we go dedicated?
[04:48] Jordan: rough ballpark: dedicated cuts per-token compute markup by ~18-25% for sustained loads due to better packing and warm cache effects. we'll post a more precise cost sheet with the raw numbers.
[04:59] Sophie: you mentioned quantization — any model quality regressions we've observed?
[05:06] Maya: on preliminary evals int8 had very small BLEU-like deltas on summarization, for clinical summarization we ran a small human spot check and didn't see actionable regressions, but we recommend a constrained eval set from your side.
[05:22] Lina: yes we'll pull 200 critical examples and run them through.
[05:27] Rajiv: on throughput: can Redwood sustain 10k tokens/sec across the cluster? our projected Q3 peak is around that range during batch runs.
[05:37] Maya: we saw linear scaling until ~6k tokens/sec on the current pool size; beyond that, we saw queueing which pushed p95. scaling is policy driven — autoscale can add slots but there's a startup window. for heavy sustained throughput, dedicated reserved capacity provides the predictability.
[05:54] Omar: startup window — how long? seconds or minutes?
[05:57] Maya: typically 90–180s to spin up a new slot and warm the cache; that's why for tight SLOs we recommend reserved or warm standby capacity.
[06:10] Jordan: happy path is: start with a 2-week dedicated slot trial to prove steady-state tails, run replay traffic, then decide on commit.
[06:21] Lina: sample results look promising, but we want to verify under our exact traffic (replay) and with our annotator mix.
[06:28] Omar: I'll provide replay creds, but need to coordinate network ACLs.
[06:33] Jordan: perfect — we'll need a short marker file and a 60-min window to run the replay.
[06:39] 
[06:39] Maya: quick note on instrumentation — we captured trace IDs and token-level timing, we'll share the annotated waterfall that highlights the top three contributors to p95 (cache miss, attention kernel swap, and occasional swap to fallback quant kernel). The waterfall is in the sheet.
[06:58] Rajiv: what was the fallback quant kernel? is it an older model fallback?
[07:03] Maya: it was an internal lower-memory path; there was a small path where, under memory pressure, the runtime switches to a less memory-hungry kernel that increases latency a bit. We've tuned thresholds but for your traffic we want to test dedicated memory headroom.
[07:18] Sophie: any blockers from Redwood's side to run the dedicated trial next week?
[07:24] Jordan: capacity is available, we just need sign-off on the window and network access. Luis will coordinate billing comms.
[07:33] Luis Ortega: I'll prepare the trial order and include options for a 2-week trial with an opt-in committed discount.
[07:41] 
[07:41] Rajiv: ok, java is a bit tight, can you put the benchmark csv into a shared drive? our infra will ingest it.
[07:48] Maya: yes, we'll push the CSV and the raw logs plus an annotated README.
[07:54] Lina: last question: have you run head-to-head under TLS + customer-managed KMS? we need to be sure encryption doesn't add a measurable tail.
[08:03] Maya: we ran a TLS+KMS run and observed negligible added latency (~12ms median), tail unaffected. we'll attach that run.
[08:13] Omar: that's good. also please include any network diagrams for peering.
[08:18] Jordan: will do.
[08:21] 
[08:21] Jordan: let's do a quick recap of next steps: Redwood — share benchmark spreadsheet, raw p95/p50 logs, annotated waterfall, SOC2 + KMS guide, and propose trial window. Helixa — provide replay creds and confirm network ACLs, pick 200 examples for quality eval.
[08:40] Rajiv: agreed. any open questions from anyone?
[08:45] Lina: none from me.
[08:47] Omar: no. thanks.
[08:49] Jordan: great, thanks everyone — we'll follow up via email with the attachments and a calendar invite for the dedicated-slot kickoff.
[08:56] End of meeting.
